en: The Sarvasāropaniṣad (The Secret Doctrine of the Essence of All)
Oṃ! May He protect us both; may He nourish us both; may we work together with vigor; may our study be brilliant; may we never harbor enmity toward one another.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.

How is there bondage? How is there liberation? What is knowledge (vidyā)? What is ignorance (avidyā)? And how are the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (turiya)? How are the sheaths (kośas) consisting of food, vital breath, mind, intellect, and bliss? How are the agent, the individual soul (jīva), the group of five, the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), the witness (sākṣin), the immutable (kūṭastha), the inner ruler (antaryāmī), the inner self (pratyagātman), and illusion (māyā)? || 1 ||

To identify the self, the Lord, the individual soul, and the non-self—such as the body and so forth—as being the self is "abhimāna" (egoistic identification), which is the bondage of the self; the cessation of that is liberation. || 2 ||
That which causes the conceit regarding that [object] is ignorance; that by which that conceit is turned back is knowledge. (3)

When the Self perceives gross objects such as sound through the fourteen instruments—the mind and the rest—which are fully developed and favored by the sun and other deities, that is the waking state of the Self. When, however, through those same fourteen instruments accompanied by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it perceives sound and other objects consisting of mere impressions even in the absence of external sound and so forth, that is the dream state of the Self. And when, due to the cessation of specific cognition arising from the fourteen instruments, it does not perceive sound and the other objects, that is the deep sleep state of the Self.

When there is a consciousness that is uninterrupted and devoid of its own objective existence, being the witness to the presence and absence of the three states, then it is called the fourth consciousness (turya-caitanya). || 4 ||

The collection of sheaths consisting of foodstuffs and the treasury [of resources] is called the *annamaya-kośa*. When the fourteen divisions of vital air (*vāyu*), beginning with *prāṇa*, reside within the *annamaya-kośa*, it is then called the *prāṇamaya-kośa*. When the Self, conjoined with these two sheaths, performs functions such as the conceptualization of objects like sound through the fourteen instruments beginning with the mind (*manas*), it is then called the *manomaya-kośa*.

When that [Self], which is attached to these three sheaths, shines forth as one who knows the specific distinctions residing therein, it is then called the "sheath consisting of consciousness" (vijñānamaya-kośa). When it exists within its own cause, ignorance (ajñāna), attached to these four sheaths—like a tree within the seed-pod—it is then called the "sheath consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya-kośa). || 5 ||

When the agent, through the cognition of pleasure and pain, reaches the end of what is beneficial—that is, when the cognition regarding a desired object is the cognition of pleasure, and the cognition regarding an undesired object is the cognition of pain—then, following the lead of meritorious and sinful karma, appearing as if entering into union with a body already obtained or as if entering into union with a body not yet obtained, he is called the "conditioned soul" (upahita-jīva). || 6 ||

The mind and so forth, the vital breaths and so forth, desire and so forth, the qualities of *sattva* and so forth, and merit and so forth—these five groups constitute the substrate (*dharmī*). Apart from the knowledge of the Self, they do not perish; while the Self is present and perceived as eternal, that which serves as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*), which is called the "knot of the heart" (*hṛd-granthi*). || 7 ||
In that context, that consciousness which shines forth is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). || 8 ||

The knower of the manifestation and disappearance of the knower, the knowledge, and the knowable—being himself devoid of manifestation and disappearance—is called the self-luminous witness (sākṣī). || 9 ||

When that which is perceived as the remainder within the intellects of all living beings, from Brahmā down to a tiny ant, abides in the intellects of all living beings, then it is called the immutable (kūṭastha). || 10 ||

When the Self is manifested as that which serves as the cause for the acquisition of their own nature by those things that are joined together through deception—pervading all fields like a thread through a collection of jewels—it is then called the "Inner Controller" (antaryāmī). || 11 ||

When the Self—truth, knowledge, infinite, blissful, and completely free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), like pure gold that remains when its adjuncts such as bracelets and crowns are removed—shines forth as having the nature of pure consciousness and intelligence alone, then that is called the referent of the word "thou" (*tvaṃpadārtha*), the inner self (*pratyagātman*). "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite. "Truth" means indestructible. That which does not perish even while space, time, objects, and causes are perishing is called "indestructible."

"Knowledge" (jñāna) refers to consciousness that is devoid of origination and destruction and is continuous; this is called knowledge. "Infinite" (ananta) refers to the consciousness that is full and all-pervading throughout the entire expansion of creation, beginning with the unmanifest—just as clay is present in its transformations, gold in its transformations, and thread in its transformations; this is called infinite. "Bliss" (ānanda) refers to the nature of conscious bliss, an immeasurable ocean of bliss, and the remaining essence of happiness; this is called bliss. || 12 ||

That whose characteristic is this fourfold reality, which is non-deviating with respect to place, time, substance, and cause—that category of existence is called the Supreme Self (paramātman). || 13 ||

You are called the Supreme Brahman—distinct from the conditioned meaning of the word "thou" (tvaṃ-padārtha) and from the conditioned difference from the meaning of the word "that" (tat-padārtha), subtle like space, and of the nature of pure existence alone. 14.

That which is called *māyā* is beginningless yet has an end; it is common to both valid and invalid means of knowledge; it is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent; it is inherently superior, devoid of modification, and when investigated, it is found to be empty of the characteristics of both existence and non-existence—this is what is termed *māyā*. It is ignorance (*ajñāna*), though insubstantial and non-existent even throughout the three periods of time; yet for the ignorant, there is a perception of reality, and for worldly people, there is the notion of its existence as "this is thus"—it is indefinable (*anirvacanīya*) and cannot be described. || 15 ||
I do not exist; I am neither the deity, nor indeed the ten senses, nor the intellect, nor the mind forever, nor likewise the ego-sense.

For I am indeed without breath and without mind, pure; for I am always the witness of the intellect and all other faculties. I am eternally pure consciousness alone—of this there is no doubt. || 17 ||
I am neither the doer nor the enjoyer; I am the witness-form of Prakṛti. Through my proximity, the body and other faculties proceed as if they were conscious. 18.
I am the Self—the eternal pillar, ever-blissful, pure, consisting of knowledge, and stainless; the all-pervading witness of all beings, without a doubt. (19)

I am Brahman alone, that which is known by all the Vedāntas; I am not the object of knowledge consisting of ether, wind, and so forth. I am neither form, nor name, nor action; I am Brahman alone, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss. || 20 ||

"I am not the body; whence can there be birth and death for me? I am not the vital breath; whence can there be hunger and thirst for me? I am not the mind; whence can there be sorrow and delusion for me? I am not the agent; whence can there be bondage and liberation for me? Thus ends the Upaniṣad. 21.
Oṃ. May He protect us both; may He nourish us both; may we work together with vigor; may our study be luminous; may we never harbor enmity toward one another.
Oṃ! Peace, peace, peace!
Thus ends the Sarvasārpaniṣad.
